claim: Ross River virus is the most important mosquito-borne disease in Australia with 1500–9500 human cases per year.
source: Here, we address these gaps by building a model for temperature-dependent transmission of Ross River virus (RRV), the most important mosquito-borne disease in Australia (1500–9500 human cases per year) (Koolhof et al., 2017), and potentially at risk of emerging worldwide (Flies et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Koolhof et al., 2017, which provides the case count data.

claim: Ross River virus is potentially at risk of emerging worldwide.
source: Here, we address these gaps by building a model for temperature-dependent transmission of Ross River virus (RRV), the most important mosquito-borne disease in Australia (1500–9500 human cases per year) (Koolhof et al., 2017), and potentially at risk of emerging worldwide (Flies et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Flies et al., 2018.

claim: RRV transmission occurs across a wide latitudinal gradient where climate varies substantially both geographically and seasonally.
source: RRV in Australia is an ideal case study for examining the influence of temperature. Transmission occurs across a wide latitudinal gradient, where climate varies substantially both geographically and seasonally.
evidence: This is a general statement about the geographic distribution of RRV transmission, drawing on established knowledge about Australia's climate variation.

claim: RRV case diagnosis and reporting are more accurate and consistent in Australia compared to vector-borne diseases in lower-income settings.
source: Moreover, compared to vector-borne diseases in lower-income settings, RRV case diagnosis and reporting are more accurate and consistent, and variation in socioeconomic conditions (and therefore housing and vector control efforts) at regional and continental scales is relatively low.
evidence: This is an inference based on general knowledge about healthcare systems in high-income versus low-income countries.

claim: In some settings temperature predicts RRV cases.
source: Previous work has shown that in some settings temperature predicts RRV cases (Gatton et al., 2005; Bi et al., 2009; Werner et al., 2012; Koolhof et al., 2017), while in others it does not (Hu et al., 2004; Gatton et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: In some settings temperature does not predict RRV cases.
source: Previous work has shown that in some settings temperature predicts RRV cases (Gatton et al., 2005; Bi et al., 2009; Werner et al., 2012; Koolhof et al., 2017), while in others it does not (Hu et al., 2004; Gatton et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2004 and Gatton et al., 2005.

claim: RRV caused an epidemic infecting over 500,000 people in Fiji in 1979–80.
source: Understanding RRV transmission ecology is critical because the virus is a candidate for emergence worldwide (Flies et al., 2018), and has caused explosive epidemics where it has emerged in the past (infecting over 500,000 people in a 1979–80 epidemic in Fiji) (Klapsing et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klapsing et al., 2005.

claim: RRV infection causes joint pain that can become chronic and cause disability.
source: RRV is a significant public health burden because infection causes joint pain that can become chronic and cause disability (Harley et al., 2001; Koolhof et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harley et al., 2001 and Koolhof et al., 2017.

claim: Thermal responses of ectotherm traits are usually unimodal: they peak at intermediate temperatures and decline towards zero at lower and upper thermal limits.
source: Thermal responses of ectotherm traits are usually unimodal: they peak at intermediate temperatures and decline towards zero at lower and upper thermal limits, all of which vary across traits (Dell et al., 2011; Mordecai et al., 2013; Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dell et al., 2011, Mordecai et al., 2013, and Mordecai et al., 2017.

claim: Mechanistic models that incorporate multiple nonlinear trait thermal responses often predict transmission optima up to 7°C lower than models that assume linear or monotonic thermal responses.
source: Synthesizing the full suite of nonlinear trait responses is critical because such models often make predictions that are drastically different, with transmission optima up to 7°C lower, than models that assume linear or monotonic thermal responses or omit temperature-dependent processes (Mordecai et al., 2013, Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mordecai et al., 2013 and Mordecai et al., 2017.

claim: The optimal temperature for falciparum malaria transmission in Anopheles vectors is 25°C.
source: Previous mechanistic models that incorporated multiple nonlinear trait thermal responses have predicted different optimal temperatures across pathogens and vector species: 25°C for falciparum malaria in Anopheles vectors (Mordecai et al., 2013) and West Nile virus in Culex vectors (Paull et al., 2017), and 29 and 26°C for dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses (in Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus, respectively) (Liu-Helmersson et al., 2014; Wesolowski et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mordecai et al., 2013.

claim: The optimal temperature for West Nile virus transmission in Culex vectors is 25°C.
source: Previous mechanistic models that incorporated multiple nonlinear trait thermal responses have predicted different optimal temperatures across pathogens and vector species: 25°C for falciparum malaria in Anopheles vectors (Mordecai et al., 2013) and West Nile virus in Culex vectors (Paull et al., 2017), and 29 and 26°C for dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses (in Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus, respectively) (Liu-Helmersson et al., 2014; Wesolowski et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Paull et al., 2017.

claim: The optimal temperature for dengue, chikungunya, and Zika virus transmission in Aedes aegypti is 29°C.
source: Previous mechanistic models that incorporated multiple nonlinear trait thermal responses have predicted different optimal temperatures across pathogens and vector species: 25°C for falciparum malaria in Anopheles vectors (Mordecai et al., 2013) and West Nile virus in Culex vectors (Paull et al., 2017), and 29 and 26°C for dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses (in Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus, respectively) (Liu-Helmersson et al., 2014; Wesolowski et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu-Helmersson et al., 2014, Wesolowski et al., 2015, and Mordecai et al., 2017.

claim: The optimal temperature for dengue, chikungunya, and Zika virus transmission in Aedes albopictus is 26°C.
source: Previous mechanistic models that incorporated multiple nonlinear trait thermal responses have predicted different optimal temperatures across pathogens and vector species: 25°C for falciparum malaria in Anopheles vectors (Mordecai et al., 2013) and West Nile virus in Culex vectors (Paull et al., 2017), and 29 and 26°C for dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses (in Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus, respectively) (Liu-Helmersson et al., 2014; Wesolowski et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu-Helmersson et al., 2014, Wesolowski et al., 2015, and Mordecai et al., 2017.

claim: Marsupials are generally considered the critical reservoirs for maintaining RRV between human outbreaks.
source: Marsupials are generally considered the critical reservoirs for maintaining the virus between human outbreaks, but recent work has argued that placental mammals and birds may be equally important in many locations (Stephenson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the general scientific consensus, with a citation to Stephenson et al., 2018 for the contrasting view.

claim: Recent work has argued that placental mammals and birds may be equally important RRV reservoirs as marsupials in many locations.
source: Marsupials are generally considered the critical reservoirs for maintaining the virus between human outbreaks, but recent work has argued that placental mammals and birds may be equally important in many locations (Stephenson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stephenson et al., 2018.

claim: RRV has been isolated from over 40 mosquito species in nature.
source: The virus has been isolated from over 40 mosquito species in nature, and 10 species transmit it in laboratory studies (Harley et al., 2001; Russell, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harley et al., 2001 and Russell, 2002.

claim: 10 mosquito species transmit RRV in laboratory studies.
source: The virus has been isolated from over 40 mosquito species in nature, and 10 species transmit it in laboratory studies (Harley et al., 2001; Russell, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harley et al., 2001 and Russell, 2002.

claim: Four mosquito species are responsible for most RRV transmission to humans: Culex annulirostris, Aedes vigilax, Ae. notoscriptus, and Ae. camptorhynchus.
source: However, four species are responsible for most transmission to humans (Culex annulirostris, Aedes [Ochlerotatus] vigilax, Ae. [O.] notoscriptus, and Ae. [O.] camptorhynchus), with two additional species implicated in outbreaks (Ae. [Stegomyia] polynesiensis and Ae. [O.] normanensis).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about RRV vectors.

claim: Two additional mosquito species have been implicated in RRV outbreaks: Ae. polynesiensis and Ae. normanensis.
source: However, four species are responsible for most transmission to humans (Culex annulirostris, Aedes [Ochlerotatus] vigilax, Ae. [O.] notoscriptus, and Ae. [O.] camptorhynchus), with two additional species implicated in outbreaks (Ae. [Stegomyia] polynesiensis and Ae. [O.] normanensis).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about RRV vectors.

claim: Ae. vigilax and Ae. notoscriptus were more commonly implicated in RRV transmission in tropical and subtropical zones.
source: Ae. vigilax and Ae. notoscriptus were more commonly implicated in transmission in tropical and subtropical zones, Ae. camptorhynchus in temperate zones, and Cx. annulirostris throughout all climatic zones.
evidence: The claim is based on data compiled from multiple outbreak reports shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ae. camptorhynchus was more commonly implicated in RRV transmission in temperate zones.
source: Ae. vigilax and Ae. notoscriptus were more commonly implicated in transmission in tropical and subtropical zones, Ae. camptorhynchus in temperate zones, and Cx. annulirostris throughout all climatic zones.
evidence: The claim is based on data compiled from multiple outbreak reports shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cx. annulirostris was implicated in RRV transmission throughout all climatic zones.
source: Ae. vigilax and Ae. notoscriptus were more commonly implicated in transmission in tropical and subtropical zones, Ae. camptorhynchus in temperate zones, and Cx. annulirostris throughout all climatic zones.
evidence: The claim is based on data compiled from multiple outbreak reports shown in Figure 1.

claim: Freshwater-breeding Cx. annulirostris has been implicated in RRV transmission across both inland and coastal areas.
source: Freshwater-breeding Cx. annulirostris has been implicated in transmission across both inland and coastal areas, while saltmarsh mosquitoes Ae. vigilax and Ae. camptorhynchus have been implicated only in coastal areas (Russell, 2002) and inland areas affected by salinization from agriculture (Biggs and Mottram, 2008; Carver et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Russell, 2002.

claim: Saltmarsh mosquitoes Ae. vigilax and Ae. camptorhynchus have been implicated in RRV transmission only in coastal areas and inland areas affected by salinization from agriculture.
source: Freshwater-breeding Cx. annulirostris has been implicated in transmission across both inland and coastal areas, while saltmarsh mosquitoes Ae. vigilax and Ae. camptorhynchus have been implicated only in coastal areas (Russell, 2002) and inland areas affected by salinization from agriculture (Biggs and Mottram, 2008; Carver et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Russell, 2002, Biggs and Mottram, 2008, and Carver et al., 2009.

claim: Peri-domestic, container-breeding Ae. notoscriptus has been implicated in urban RRV epidemics.
source: Peri-domestic, container-breeding Ae. notoscriptus has been implicated in urban epidemics (Russell, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Russell, 2002.

claim: Ae. camptorhynchus populations peak earlier and in cooler temperatures than Ae. vigilax.
source: The vectors also differ in their seasonality: Ae. camptorhynchus populations peak earlier and in cooler temperatures than Ae. vigilax, leading to seasonal succession where they overlap (Yang et al., 2009; Russell, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2009 and Russell, 1998.

claim: Ae. camptorhynchus and Ae. vigilax show seasonal succession where they overlap.
source: The vectors also differ in their seasonality: Ae. camptorhynchus populations peak earlier and in cooler temperatures than Ae. vigilax, leading to seasonal succession where they overlap (Yang et al., 2009; Russell, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2009 and Russell, 1998.

claim: Vector and pathogen traits that drive RRV transmission consistently responded to temperature.
source: Vector and pathogen traits that drive transmission consistently responded to temperature (Figure 2), though data were sparse (McDonald et al., 1980; Mottram et al., 1986; Russell, 1986; Rae, 1990; Kay and Jennings, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and citations to the source studies.

claim: No Australian RRV vector species had data for all necessary traits at three or more constant temperatures.
source: Although we exhaustively searched for experiments with trait measurements at three or more constant temperatures in the Australian vector species (Cx. annulirostris, Ae. vigilax, Ae. camptorhynchus, Ae. notoscriptus, and Ae. normanensis), no species had data for all necessary traits (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is based on an exhaustive literature search and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Thermal optima for RRV-related traits ranged from 23.4°C for adult lifespan to 33.0°C for parasite development rate.
source: Thermal optima ranged from 23.4°C for adult lifespan (lf) to 33.0°C for parasite development rate (PDR; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on the fitted thermal response curves shown in Figure 2.

claim: The data supported unimodal thermal responses for most RRV-related traits.
source: The data supported unimodal thermal responses for most traits, though declines at high temperatures were not directly observed for biting rate (a) and parasite development rate.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Declines at high temperatures were not directly observed for biting rate and parasite development rate.
source: The data supported unimodal thermal responses for most traits, though declines at high temperatures were not directly observed for biting rate (a) and parasite development rate.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the available data.

claim: RRV transmission potential (relative R0) peaked at 26.4°C.
source: Transmission potential (relative R0 from the full R0 model) peaked at 26.4°C, and was positive from 17.0–31.5°C (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on the model results shown in Figure 3.

claim: RRV transmission potential was positive from 17.0–31.5°C.
source: Transmission potential (relative R0 from the full R0 model) peaked at 26.4°C, and was positive from 17.0–31.5°C (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on the model results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Removing the temperature-dependence of mosquito density did not substantially affect the peak temperature for RRV transmission.
source: Removing the temperature-dependence of mosquito density [M] did not substantially affect the peak, because the optima for transmission and mosquito density were closely aligned (constant M model: 26.6°C, M: 26.2°C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparing model results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The range of temperatures suitable for RRV transmission is much larger when mosquito density does not depend on temperature (12.9–33.7°C vs 17.0–31.5°C).
source: By contrast, the range of temperatures suitable for transmission is much larger when mosquito density does not depend on temperature because M(T) constrains transmission at the thermal limits (constant M model positive from 12.9–33.7°C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparing model results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The moderate optimal temperature for RRV (26–27°C) fits within the range of thermal optima found for other diseases.
source: The moderate optimal temperature for RRV (26–27°C) fits within the range of thermal optima found for other diseases: malaria transmission by Anopheles spp. at 25°C, and dengue and other viruses by Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus at 29 and 26°C, respectively (Figure 4) (Mordecai et al., 2013; Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on comparing the RRV model results with previously published models, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: At the upper thermal limit, fecundity and adult lifespan constrain RRV R0.
source: At the upper thermal limit fecundity (EFD) and adult lifespan (lf) constrain R0, while at the lower thermal limit fecundity, larval survival (pLA), egg survival (raft viability [pRH] and survival within rafts [nLR]), and adult lifespan constrain R0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: At the lower thermal limit, fecundity, larval survival, egg survival, and adult lifespan constrain RRV R0.
source: At the upper thermal limit fecundity (EFD) and adult lifespan (lf) constrain R0, while at the lower thermal limit fecundity, larval survival (pLA), egg survival (raft viability [pRH] and survival within rafts [nLR]), and adult lifespan constrain R0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The optimal temperature for RRV R0 was most sensitive to the thermal response of adult lifespan.
source: The optimal temperature for R0 was most sensitive to the thermal response of adult lifespan.
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Near the optimum, most uncertainty in RRV R0 was due to uncertainty in the thermal responses of biting rate and egg raft viability.
source: Near the optimum, most uncertainty in R0 was due to uncertainty in the thermal responses of biting rate and egg raft viability.
evidence: The claim is based on uncertainty analysis results.

claim: Substituting larval traits from alternative vectors or infection traits for Murray Valley Encephalitis virus did not substantially alter the RRV R0 thermal response.
source: For comparison, substituting larval traits from alternative vectors or infection traits for Murray Valley Encephalitis virus did not substantially alter the R0 thermal response, since Cx. annulirostris life history traits strongly constrained transmission (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on model comparison results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In subtropical and temperate locations (Brisbane and further south), low temperatures force RRV R0 to zero for part of the year.
source: In subtropical and temperate locations (Brisbane and further south), low temperatures force R0 to zero for part of the year (Figures 5A and 6).
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: In tropical, northern Australia (Darwin and Cairns), the temperature remains suitable for RRV transmission throughout the year.
source: By contrast, in tropical, northern Australia (Darwin and Cairns), the temperature remains suitable throughout the year (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Darwin is the only major Australian city where mean temperatures exceed the thermal optimum for RRV transmission.
source: Darwin is the only major city where mean temperatures exceed the thermal optimum, and thereby depress transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on comparing temperature data with model predictions.

claim: Human RRV cases peak two months after population-weighted R0(T) at the national scale.
source: Using the average (1992–2013) seasonal incidence at the national scale, human cases peak two months after population-weighted R0(T), matching our a priori hypothesized time lag between temperature suitability and human cases (based on empirical work in other mosquito-borne disease systems, see Materials and methods and Discussion; Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on comparing model predictions with case data shown in Figure 7.

claim: RRV is endemic in tropical Australia with little seasonal variation in transmission potential due to temperature.
source: As predicted by the model (Figures 5 and 6), RRV is endemic in tropical Australia, with little seasonal variation in transmission potential due to temperature, and seasonally epidemic in subtropical and temperate Australia (Weinstein, 1997).
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions and supported by a citation to Weinstein, 1997.

claim: RRV is seasonally epidemic in subtropical and temperate Australia.
source: As predicted by the model (Figures 5 and 6), RRV is endemic in tropical Australia, with little seasonal variation in transmission potential due to temperature, and seasonally epidemic in subtropical and temperate Australia (Weinstein, 1997).
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions and supported by a citation to Weinstein, 1997.

claim: RRV transmission by Cx. annulirostris in inland areas often moves south as temperatures increase from spring into summer.
source: Further, RRV transmission by Cx. annulirostris in inland areas often moves south as temperatures increase from spring into summer (Russell, 1998), matching the model prediction (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Russell, 1998 and matches model predictions.

claim: RRV incidence is often—but not always—positively associated with warmer temperatures.
source: Specifically, statistical evidence for temperature impacts on local time series of cases is mixed. RRV incidence is often—but not always—positively associated with warmer temperatures (Tong and Hu, 2001; Tong et al., 2002a; Tong et al., 2004; Hu et al., 2004; Hu et al., 2010; Jacups et al., 2008b, Williams et al., 2009; Werner et al., 2012; Koolhof et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous statistical studies.

claim: RRV outbreaks were less likely with more days above 35°C in part of Queensland.
source: Although field-based evidence for unimodal thermal responses in vector-borne disease is rare (but see Mordecai et al., 2013; Perkins et al., 2015; Peña-García et al., 2017), there is some evidence for high temperatures constraining RRV transmission and vector populations: outbreaks were less likely with more days above 35°C in part of Queensland (Gatton et al., 2005) and populations of Cx. annulirostris peaked at 25°C and declined above 32°C in Victoria (Dhileepan, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gatton et al., 2005.

claim: Populations of Cx. annulirostris peaked at 25°C and declined above 32°C in Victoria.
source: Although field-based evidence for unimodal thermal responses in vector-borne disease is rare (but see Mordecai et al., 2013; Perkins et al., 2015; Peña-García et al., 2017), there is some evidence for high temperatures constraining RRV transmission and vector populations: outbreaks were less likely with more days above 35°C in part of Queensland (Gatton et al., 2005) and populations of Cx. annulirostris peaked at 25°C and declined above 32°C in Victoria (Dhileepan, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dhileepan, 1996.

claim: Local rainfall or river flow have been linked to the abundance of RRV vector species.
source: Breeding habitat availability also drives mosquito abundance and mosquito-borne disease. Local rainfall or river flow have been linked to the abundance of RRV vector species (Barton et al., 2004; Tall et al., 2014; Jacups et al., 2015) and RRV disease cases (Tong and Hu, 2001; Tong et al., 2002a; Hu et al., 2004; Kelly-Hope et al., 2004b; Tong et al., 2004; Gatton et al., 2005; Jacups et al., 2008b; Bi et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2009; Werner et al., 2012), as have high tides in coastal areas with saltmarsh mosquitoes, Ae. vigilax and Ae. camptorhynchus (Tong and Hu, 2002b; Tong et al., 2004; Jacups et al., 2008b; Kokkinn et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barton et al., 2004, Tall et al., 2014, and Jacups et al., 2015.

claim: Local rainfall or river flow have been linked to RRV disease cases.
source: Breeding habitat availability also drives mosquito abundance and mosquito-borne disease. Local rainfall or river flow have been linked to the abundance of RRV vector species (Barton et al., 2004; Tall et al., 2014; Jacups et al., 2015) and RRV disease cases (Tong and Hu, 2001; Tong et al., 2002a; Hu et al., 2004; Kelly-Hope et al., 2004b; Tong et al., 2004; Gatton et al., 2005; Jacups et al., 2008b; Bi et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2009; Werner et al., 2012), as have high tides in coastal areas with saltmarsh mosquitoes, Ae. vigilax and Ae. camptorhynchus (Tong and Hu, 2002b; Tong et al., 2004; Jacups et al., 2008b; Kokkinn et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: High tides in coastal areas have been linked to RRV cases in areas with saltmarsh mosquitoes Ae. vigilax and Ae. camptorhynchus.
source: Breeding habitat availability also drives mosquito abundance and mosquito-borne disease. Local rainfall or river flow have been linked to the abundance of RRV vector species (Barton et al., 2004; Tall et al., 2014; Jacups et al., 2015) and RRV disease cases (Tong and Hu, 2001; Tong et al., 2002a; Hu et al., 2004; Kelly-Hope et al., 2004b; Tong et al., 2004; Gatton et al., 2005; Jacups et al., 2008b; Bi et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2009; Werner et al., 2012), as have high tides in coastal areas with saltmarsh mosquitoes, Ae. vigilax and Ae. camptorhynchus (Tong and Hu, 2002b; Tong et al., 2004; Jacups et al., 2008b; Kokkinn et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tong and Hu, 2002b, Tong et al., 2004, Jacups et al., 2008b, and Kokkinn et al., 2009.

claim: In Western Australia, heavy summer rains can fail to initiate RRV epidemics when low rainfall in the preceding winter depresses recruitment of susceptible juvenile kangaroos.
source: For instance, in Western Australia heavy summer rains can fail to initiate epidemics when low rainfall in the preceding winter depresses recruitment of susceptible juvenile kangaroos (Mackenzie et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mackenzie et al., 2000.

claim: Large RRV outbreaks occur in southeastern Australia when high rainfall follows a dry year, presumably from higher transmission within relatively unexposed reservoir populations.
source: By contrast, large outbreaks occur in southeastern Australia when high rainfall follows a dry year, presumably from higher transmission within relatively unexposed reservoir populations (Woodruff et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Woodruff et al., 2002.

claim: Climate warming will likely increase RRV transmission in temperate, southern Australia where most Australians live.
source: Climate warming will likely increase the geographic and seasonal range of transmission potential in temperate, southern Australia where most Australians live.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model results and inference about climate change impacts.

claim: Climate change will likely decrease RRV transmission potential in tropical areas like Darwin.
source: However, climate change will likely decrease transmission potential in tropical areas like Darwin, where moderate warming (~3°C) would push temperatures above the upper thermal limit for transmission for most of the year (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model results shown in Figure 5 and inference about climate change impacts.

claim: Moderate warming (~3°C) in Darwin would push temperatures above the upper thermal limit for RRV transmission for most of the year.
source: However, climate change will likely decrease transmission potential in tropical areas like Darwin, where moderate warming (~3°C) would push temperatures above the upper thermal limit for transmission for most of the year (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model results and climate change scenarios.

claim: The moderate optimal temperature for RRV (26–27°C) was largely determined by the thermal response of adult mosquito lifespan.
source: The moderate optimal temperature for RRV (26–27°C) fit within the range of thermal optima found for other diseases using the same methods: malaria transmission by Anopheles spp. at 25°C, and dengue and other viruses by Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus at 29 and 26°C, respectively (Figure 4) (Mordecai et al., 2013; Mordecai et al., 2017). For all of these diseases, the specific optimal temperature was largely determined by the thermal response of adult lifespan (Mordecai et al., 2013,;Mordecai et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis and comparison with other disease systems.

claim: For malaria, dengue, and RRV, the specific optimal temperature was largely determined by the thermal response of adult lifespan.
source: The moderate optimal temperature for RRV (26–27°C) fit within the range of thermal optima found for other diseases using the same methods: malaria transmission by Anopheles spp. at 25°C, and dengue and other viruses by Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus at 29 and 26°C, respectively (Figure 4) (Mordecai et al., 2013; Mordecai et al., 2017). For all of these diseases, the specific optimal temperature was largely determined by the thermal response of adult lifespan (Mordecai et al., 2013,;Mordecai et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mordecai et al., 2013, Mordecai et al., 2017, and Johnson et al., 2015.

claim: The lower thermal limit for RRV was constrained by fecundity and survival at all stages.
source: However, the traits that set the thermal limits for RRV transmission differed from other systems. The lower thermal limit for RRV was constrained by fecundity and survival at all stages, while the upper thermal limit was constrained by fecundity and adult lifespan.
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis results.

claim: The upper thermal limit for RRV was constrained by fecundity and adult lifespan.
source: However, the traits that set the thermal limits for RRV transmission differed from other systems. The lower thermal limit for RRV was constrained by fecundity and survival at all stages, while the upper thermal limit was constrained by fecundity and adult lifespan.
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Thermal limits for malaria transmission were set by parasite development rate at cool temperatures and egg-to-adulthood survival at high temperatures.
source: By contrast, thermal limits for malaria transmission were set by parasite development rate at cool temperatures and egg-to-adulthood survival at high temperatures (Mordecai et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mordecai et al., 2013.

claim: The upper and lower thermal limits of RRV transmission are more uncertain than the optimum.
source: As with previous models, the upper and lower thermal limits of RRV transmission are more uncertain than the optimum (Figure 3) (Johnson et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2017), because trait responses are harder to measure near their thermal limits where survival is low and development is slow or incomplete.
evidence: The claim is based on uncertainty analysis and supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2015 and Mordecai et al., 2017.

claim: Upper thermal limits of mosquito-borne disease transmission are primarily determined by vector life history traits with symmetrical thermal performance curves rather than rate-based traits with asymmetrical thermal performance curves.
source: Additionally, upper thermal limits of mosquito-borne disease transmission (a major concern for climate change) are primarily determined by vector life history traits with symmetrical thermal performance curves (like fecundity and survival at various life stages) rather than rate-based traits with asymmetrical thermal performance curves (like biting rate or pathogen development rate).
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the analysis of RRV and comparison with other disease systems.

claim: Two RRV-related traits (fecundity and adult lifespan) had data from only three temperatures.
source: The trait thermal response data were limited in two keys ways. First, two traits (fecundity and adult lifespan) had data from only three temperatures.
